content: Magnesium sulphate is widely utilized in obstetrics for the treatment and prevention of eclampsia. Recent meta-analyses have demonstrated that magnesium sulphate, when administered antenatally to women at risk of very preterm birth, serves as an effective neuroprotective agent for the fetus. Term infants, who represent more than half of all cases of cerebral palsy, have shown a relatively stable incidence of this condition over time. It is therefore critical to evaluate whether antenatal administration of magnesium sulphate to women at term can protect the fetus from brain injury and associated neurosensory disabilities, including cerebral palsy. The objective of this study was to assess the effectiveness of magnesium sulphate, administered to women at term, as a neuroprotective agent for the fetus. To achieve this, a systematic search was conducted in the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Group's Trial Register (as of July 31, 2012) and in the reference lists of other Cochrane reviews that evaluated magnesium sulphate use during pregnancy. The inclusion criteria for this review were randomized controlled trials comparing antenatal administration of magnesium sulphate to women at term with either a placebo, no treatment, or an alternative fetal neuroprotective agent. Cluster-randomized trials were also considered for inclusion, while cross-over trials, quasi-randomized trials, and studies reported only as abstracts were excluded. Two independent reviewers assessed the eligibility of trials and evaluated the risk of bias. Data extraction was performed independently by two authors, and the extracted data were cross-checked for accuracy. The review included one trial involving 135 women with mild pre-eclampsia at term. An additional six studies are awaiting further assessment. The included trial compared magnesium sulphate with a placebo and was determined to have a low risk of bias. However, this trial did not report any of the primary outcomes pre-specified in the review. There was no significant difference between the magnesium sulphate and placebo groups in terms of Apgar scores below seven at five minutes (risk ratio [RR] 0.51; 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.05 to 5.46; 135 infants) or gestational age at birth (mean difference [MD] -0.20 weeks; 95% CI -0.62 to 0.22; 135 infants). However, significantly more maternal side effects, such as feelings of warmth and flushing, were reported in the magnesium sulphate group compared to the placebo group (RR 3.81; 95% CI 2.22 to 6.53; 135 women). Despite this, no significant difference was observed in the rate of adverse effects severe enough to necessitate discontinuation of treatment (RR 3.04; 95% CI 0.13 to 73.42; 135 women). Additionally, no significant differences were observed between the magnesium sulphate and placebo groups in the rates of postpartum hemorrhage (RR 4.06; 95% CI 0.47 to 35.38; 135 women) or cesarean section (RR 0.80; 95% CI 0.39 to 1.63; 135 women). In conclusion, there is currently insufficient evidence to determine the efficacy and safety of magnesium sulphate when administered to women at term for fetal neuroprotection. While recent evidence supports the use of magnesium sulphate for neuroprotection in preterm fetuses, high-quality randomized controlled trials are necessary to evaluate its safety profile and neurological outcomes for term fetuses. Furthermore, strategies to mitigate maternal side effects during treatment require further investigation.
